pos: n. (a Cistercian abbey in Perthshire, founded 1162 by Malcolm IV; the richest house of the order in Scotland)
etymology: Gaelic comhpairt or Pictish cupar, a confluence or common holding, with Angus, the ancient province — distinguished from Cupar in Fife.
biblical_def: Coupar Angus was founded in 1162 by Malcolm IV on the fertile carse of Gowrie, a daughter of Melrose, and it became the wealthiest Cistercian house in Scotland. Its rental books survive and show a great agricultural corporation: granges, mills, salmon fishings, coal, peat, and hundreds of tenants. By the sixteenth century its revenues were being drawn by commendators who were not monks at all, and at the Reformation the lands passed into a temporal lordship. Wealth is not the sin here; the failure to notice it is. Moses put the danger in the exact order in which it comes: “Lest when thou hast eaten and art full, and hast built goodly houses, and dwelt therein” (Deu 8:12), and then “Then thine heart be lifted up, and thou forget the LORD thy God” (Deu 8:14), and finally the sentence a prosperous institution says without hearing itself say it: “My power and the might of mine hand hath gotten me this wealth” (Deu 8:17). The remedy Moses gives is not poverty but memory, for it is God “that giveth thee power to get wealth” (Deu 8:18).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines wealth as prosperity, external happiness, and riches, large possessions of money, goods or land; and prosperity as advance or gain in any thing good or desirable.
webster_full: WEALTH, n. Prosperity; external happiness. Riches; large possessions of money, goods or land; that abundance of worldly estate which exceeds the estate of the greater part of the community.
PROSPERITY, n. Advance or gain in any thing good or desirable; successful progress in any business or enterprise; attainment of the object desired.
GRANGE, n. A farm, with the buildings, stables, etc.; a farm house with the adjoining buildings.
RENTAL, n. A schedule or account of rents, with the tenants names and the like; a rent roll.
FORGET, v.t. To lose the remembrance of; to let go from the memory.
scriptures: Deu 8:12
Lest when thou hast eaten and art full, and hast built goodly houses, and dwelt therein;
Deu 8:14
Then thine heart be lifted up, and thou forget the LORD thy God, which brought thee forth out of the land of Egypt, from the house of bondage;
Deu 8:17
And thou say in thine heart, My power and the might of mine hand hath gotten me this wealth.
Deu 8:18
But thou shalt remember the LORD thy God: for it is he that giveth thee power to get wealth, that he may establish his covenant which he sware unto thy fathers, as it is this day.
corruption_summary: The richest Cistercian house in Scotland, and the order in which Moses says prosperity destroys a people.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the slow conversion of a religious house into an estate, which happened at Coupar Angus so completely that the last men to hold its title were laymen holding it for the rent. No single decision caused it. Moses describes the mechanism as forgetting, which is passive and takes a generation, and he puts it immediately after eating and building — the two most ordinary goods there are.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the remedy for the danger of wealth is remembrance, not renunciation. “But thou shalt remember the LORD thy God: for it is he that giveth thee power to get wealth” (Deu 8:18) leaves the wealth in the hands and changes the account of where it came from. A congregation with a large endowment is not thereby corrupt; a congregation that has stopped saying that sentence is already on the road.
roots_summary: Pictish cupar, a confluence; Hebrew sabea (H7646), to be satisfied or full; Hebrew rum (H7311), to be lifted up; Hebrew shakach (H7911), to forget; Hebrew chayil (H2428), strength or wealth.
roots_lines: Pictish cupar — a confluence or common holding, with the province of Angus.
Hebrew sabea (H7646) — to be sated, filled; “when thou hast eaten and art full” (Deu 8:12).
Hebrew rum (H7311) — to be high, to be lifted up; “Then thine heart be lifted up” (Deu 8:14).
Hebrew shakach (H7911) — to forget; “and thou forget the LORD thy God” (Deu 8:14).
Hebrew chayil (H2428) — strength, might, wealth; “power to get wealth” (Deu 8:18).
usage: “and hast built goodly houses, and dwelt therein” (Deu 8:12) — the carse of Gowrie in 1500.
“My power and the might of mine hand” (Deu 8:17) — what a rental book says silently.
“But thou shalt remember the LORD thy God” (Deu 8:18) — the only remedy prescribed.

pos: n. (a Cistercian abbey in Aberdeenshire, founded 1219 by William Comyn; successor in name to the Celtic monastery whose Book of Deer holds the oldest written Scottish Gaelic)
etymology: Gaelic Deara, of uncertain sense, perhaps from doire, an oak grove; the Cistercian house took the name of the older Celtic monastery nearby.
biblical_def: Deer Abbey was founded in 1219 by William Comyn, earl of Buchan, as a daughter of Kinloss. Its greater interest lies in what it inherited the name of. The earlier Celtic monastery of Deer owned a small tenth-century gospel book, and in its margins, in the eleventh and twelfth centuries, someone wrote down in Gaelic the grants of land the house had received. Those notes are the oldest surviving writing in Scottish Gaelic, and they survive because they were written in the margin of a book that was kept because it was Scripture. The pattern is the Bible's own. Moses commands that the law be deposited where it cannot be lost: “Take this book of the law, and put it in the side of the ark of the covenant of the LORD your God, that it may be there for a witness against thee” (Deu 31:26). Isaiah is told the same, “note it in a book, that it may be for the time to come for ever and ever” (Isa 30:8). A nation's earliest words were preserved in the margins of the only book anyone thought worth keeping.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines margin as the border, brink, edge, the edge of a page left blank or filled with notes; and witness as testimony, attestation of a fact or event.
webster_full: MARGIN, n. A border; brink; edge; verge; as the margin of a river or lake. The edge of a page left blank or filled with notes.
WITNESS, n. Testimony; attestation of a fact or event. That which furnishes evidence or proof.
CHARTER, n. A written instrument, executed with usual forms, given as evidence of a grant, contract, or whatever is done between man and man.
VERNACULAR, a. Native; belonging to the country of one's birth; as one's vernacular tongue.
GOSPEL, n. The history of the birth, life, actions, death, resurrection, ascension and doctrines of Jesus Christ.
scriptures: Take this book of the law, and put it in the side of the ark of the covenant of the LORD your God, that it may be there for a witness against thee.
Isa 30:8
Now go, write it before them in a table, and note it in a book, that it may be for the time to come for ever and ever:

And Joshua said unto all the people, Behold, this stone shall be a witness unto us; for it hath heard all the words of the LORD which he spake unto us: it shall be therefore a witness unto you, lest ye deny your God.
Hab 2:2
And the LORD answered me, and said, Write the vision, and make it plain upon tables, that he may run that readeth it.
corruption_summary: A Cistercian house that took the name of an older Celtic monastery, whose gospel book preserved a language in its margins.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the loss of what was never written down. The Celtic church of the north left little, and what we have of its land, its speech and its grants comes from scribbles in a book's borders. Scripture repeatedly orders the writing precisely against that loss, and gives the reason: “Write the vision, and make it plain upon tables, that he may run that readeth it” (Hab 2:2). A memory held only in men dies with them.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the written word stands as a witness against the community that keeps it, not merely for it. “that it may be there for a witness against thee” (Deu 31:26) is a startling reason to preserve a book, and Joshua says the same of a stone: “it hath heard all the words of the LORD which he spake unto us” (Jos 24:27). A church that keeps Scripture has kept its own indictment, which is exactly why it is safe to keep it.
roots_summary: Gaelic doire, an oak grove; Hebrew cepher (H5612), a book; Hebrew ed (H5707), a witness; Hebrew kathab (H3789), to write; Hebrew baar (H874), to make plain.
roots_lines: Gaelic doire — an oak grove; the probable root of Deer.
Hebrew cepher (H5612) — a book, a written document; “Take this book of the law” (Deu 31:26).
Hebrew ed (H5707) — a witness; “for a witness against thee” (Deu 31:26).
Hebrew kathab (H3789) — to write, to inscribe; “and note it in a book” (Isa 30:8).
Hebrew baar (H874) — to make distinct, to engrave plainly; “make it plain upon tables” (Hab 2:2).
usage: “that it may be for the time to come for ever and ever” (Isa 30:8) — why marginal notes outlive abbeys.
“that he may run that readeth it” (Hab 2:2) — the standard for plain writing.
“this stone shall be a witness unto us” (Jos 24:27) — the same office, in stone.

pos: n. (a Cistercian abbey in Galloway, founded 1273 by Devorgilla of Galloway in memory of her husband; Latin Dulce Cor)
etymology: A translation of the Latin Dulce Cor, sweet heart, the name the monks gave the house because its foundress was buried with her husband's embalmed heart.
biblical_def: Sweetheart Abbey at New Abbey in Galloway was founded in 1273 by Devorgilla, lady of Galloway, in memory of her husband John Balliol, who had died earlier that year. She had his heart embalmed and kept it with her in an ivory casket for the rest of her life; when she died in 1290 she was buried before the high altar with it on her breast, and the monks named the house Dulce Cor. The red sandstone church still stands roofless and nearly complete. It is the most affecting foundation story in Britain, and Scripture does not sentimentalise what it describes but it does not belittle it either. “Set me as a seal upon thine heart, as a seal upon thine arm: for love is strong as death” (Son 8:6) is the nearest thing in Scripture to what Devorgilla did, and the verse that follows refuses to price it: “Many waters cannot quench love, neither can the floods drown it: if a man would give all the substance of his house for love, it would utterly be contemned” (Son 8:7). She gave the substance of her house, and the Song says the love was still not bought.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines seal as a piece of metal or other hard substance on which is engraved a figure or device, used to make an impression; and memorial as that which preserves the memory of something.
webster_full: SEAL, n. A piece of metal or other hard substance, usually round or oval, on which is engraved some image or device, and sometimes a legend or inscription, used by individuals and by corporations.
MEMORIAL, n. That which preserves the memory of something; any thing that serves to keep in memory.
HEART, n. A muscular viscus, which is the primary organ of the blood's motion. The seat of the affections and passions.
EMBALM, v.t. To open a dead body, take out the intestines, and fill their place with odoriferous and desiccative spices and drugs, to prevent its putrefaction.
DEVOTION, n. The state of being dedicated, consecrated, or solemnly set apart for a particular purpose. Ardent love or affection; attachment manifested by constant attention.
scriptures: Son 8:6
Set me as a seal upon thine heart, as a seal upon thine arm: for love is strong as death; jealousy is cruel as the grave: the coals thereof are coals of fire, which hath a most vehement flame.
Son 8:7
Many waters cannot quench love, neither can the floods drown it: if a man would give all the substance of his house for love, it would utterly be contemned.
And thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thy heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy mind, and with all thy strength: this is the first commandment.
Ecc 9:6
Also their love, and their hatred, and their envy, is now perished; neither have they any more a portion for ever in any thing that is done under the sun.
corruption_summary: The abbey called Sweet Heart, founded by a widow who kept her husband's heart in a casket for seventeen years.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption, if it is one, lies in what an endowment of this kind was understood to purchase: not only a memorial but masses, and with them a shortening of a dead man's suffering. The grief is real and the doctrine is false, and it is important to keep the two apart. The Preacher states the hard fact that no foundation can alter: “neither have they any more a portion for ever in any thing that is done under the sun” (Ecc 9:6).

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the direction of first love. “And thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thy heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy mind, and with all thy strength: this is the first commandment” (Mar 12:30) orders the affections without destroying them; a widow who loved a husband that way may yet have loved God first, and the dictionary has no means of knowing. What it can say is that the Song's seal is set upon the living heart, and that love which is strong as death still cannot pass it.
roots_summary: Latin Dulce Cor, sweet heart; Hebrew chotham (H2368), a seal; Hebrew ahabah (H160), love; Hebrew qinah (H7068), jealousy or ardour; Hebrew leb (H3820), the heart.
roots_lines: Latin Dulce Cor — sweet heart, the monks' name for the house.
Hebrew chotham (H2368) — a signet, a seal; “Set me as a seal upon thine heart” (Son 8:6).
Hebrew ahabah (H160) — love; “for love is strong as death” (Son 8:6).
Hebrew qinah (H7068) — ardour, jealousy; “jealousy is cruel as the grave” (Son 8:6).
Hebrew leb (H3820) — the heart, the inner man; “with all thy heart” (Mar 12:30).
usage: “which hath a most vehement flame” (Son 8:6) — the Song's word for what she did.
“Many waters cannot quench love” (Son 8:7) — and seventeen years did not.
“this is the first commandment” (Mar 12:30) — the order the affections must keep.

pos: n. (a Cistercian abbey in Kintyre, Argyll, founded about 1160 by Somerled or his son Ragnall; keeper of a famous set of West Highland warrior grave-slabs)
etymology: Norse sand-dalr, the sandy valley, or Gaelic Saghadail — the abbey in the valley on the Kintyre coast.
biblical_def: Saddell was founded about 1160 in Kintyre by Somerled, lord of Argyll and the Isles, or by his son Ragnall, and Somerled is said to be buried there. Little stands, but the site holds one of the finest collections of late medieval West Highland grave-slabs in Scotland: full-length carved warriors in quilted armour, their two-handed swords running the length of the stone, with galleys and hunting scenes around them. A monastery whose most famous possession is a row of armed men in effigy raises a question Scripture answers twice over. The first answer is the promise: “they shall beat their swords into plowshares, and their spears into pruninghooks: nation shall not lift up sword against nation, neither shall they learn war any more” (Isa 2:4). The second is the confession that makes it possible: “Some trust in chariots, and some in horses: but we will remember the name of the LORD our God” (Psa 20:7). The Psalmist does not say the chariots are useless. He says the trust is misplaced, and he is speaking as a king who went to war.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines effigy as the image or likeness of a person, a representation as on coins or monuments; and sword as an offensive weapon worn at the side, used for cutting or thrusting.
webster_full: EFFIGY, n. The image or likeness of a person; resemblance; representation; as on coins or monuments.
SWORD, n. An offensive weapon worn at the side, and used by hand either for thrusting or cutting.
MONUMENT, n. Any thing by which the memory of a person or of an event is preserved or perpetuated; a building, stone, or other thing placed or erected to remind men of the person who raised it.
GALLEY, n. A low flat built vessel with one deck, and navigated with sails and oars.
CHARIOT, n. A half coach; a carriage with four wheels and one seat behind, used for convenience and pleasure. A car used in war.
scriptures: Isa 2:4

And he shall judge among the nations, and shall rebuke many people: and they shall beat their swords into plowshares, and their spears into pruninghooks: nation shall not lift up sword against nation, neither shall they learn war any more.
Psa 20:7
Some trust in chariots, and some in horses: but we will remember the name of the LORD our God.
Psa 46:9
He maketh wars to cease unto the end of the earth; he breaketh the bow, and cutteth the spear in sunder; he burneth the chariot in the fire.
Psa 44:6
For I will not trust in my bow, neither shall my sword save me.
corruption_summary: An abbey whose treasures are carved warriors with two-handed swords, and the psalm that will not call them useless or trust them.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the baptism of the warrior ideal — a church that becomes the chaplaincy of a fighting aristocracy and carves its patrons in armour on the floor of the choir. The Highlands are not unique in this and the Reformation did not end it. Scripture permits the magistrate the sword and still refuses the trust: “For I will not trust in my bow, neither shall my sword save me” (Psa 44:6) is said by the same people who fought.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the eschatology that makes peace a future fact rather than a sentiment. “He maketh wars to cease unto the end of the earth; he breaketh the bow, and cutteth the spear in sunder” (Psa 46:9) is God's act, not a programme, and until he performs it the slabs at Saddell are an honest record of what men are.
roots_summary: Norse sand-dalr, sandy valley; Hebrew chereb (H2719), a sword; Hebrew eth (H855), a plowshare; Hebrew rekeb (H7393), a chariot; Hebrew batach (H982), to trust.
roots_lines: Norse sand-dalr — the sandy valley on the Kintyre coast.
Hebrew chereb (H2719) — a sword; “nation shall not lift up sword against nation” (Isa 2:4).
Hebrew eth (H855) — a plowshare, a mattock; “they shall beat their swords into plowshares” (Isa 2:4).
Hebrew rekeb (H7393) — a chariot; “Some trust in chariots, and some in horses” (Psa 20:7).
Hebrew batach (H982) — to trust, to rely on; “For I will not trust in my bow” (Psa 44:6).
usage: “neither shall they learn war any more” (Isa 2:4) — the promise over a row of armed slabs.
“but we will remember the name of the LORD our God” (Psa 20:7) — the soldier's confession.
“he burneth the chariot in the fire” (Psa 46:9) — whose act peace is.

pos: n. (a Premonstratensian abbey in Essex, moved to its site near Maldon in 1180; its chapter house and dorter survive within a later private house)
etymology: Old English beo, a bee, with leah, a clearing — the bee clearing, by the Chelmer near Maldon.
biblical_def: Beeleigh was founded at Great Parndon about 1172 and moved to the water-meadows near Maldon in 1180, a house of Premonstratensian canons — the white canons, who followed a rule of Augustine under a Cistercian-style discipline and served parish churches as well as keeping the office. At the dissolution the church was pulled down, but the chapter house, with its vaulted roof on Purbeck marble shafts, and the dorter above it, were taken into a private house and stand today. The chapter house was where the community met daily to hear the rule read and to correct one another, which is the part of monastic practice nearest to a New Testament ordinance. “But exhort one another daily, while it is called To day; lest any of you be hardened through the deceitfulness of sin” (Heb 3:13) describes the business done in that room, and Paul makes it mutual and verbal: “teaching and admonishing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs” (Col 3:16). What makes it possible is the thing the canons also had, a rule read aloud so that correction was by a standard and not by preference.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines chapter as an assembly of monks or of the clergy of a cathedral; and admonish as to warn or notify of a fault, to reprove with mildness.
webster_full: CHAPTER, n. A division of a book or writing. An assembly of monks, or of the prebends or clergy of a cathedral or collegiate church.
ADMONISH, v.t. To warn or notify of a fault; to reprove with mildness.
DORTER, n. A dormitory; a sleeping room, or a building containing a series of sleeping apartments.
EXHORT, v.t. To incite by words or advice; to animate or urge by arguments to a good deed or to any laudable conduct.
CANON, n. A dignitary of the church; a person who possesses a prebend or revenue allotted for the performance of divine service.
scriptures: Heb 3:13
But exhort one another daily, while it is called To day; lest any of you be hardened through the deceitfulness of sin.
Col 3:16
Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly in all wisdom; teaching and admonishing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing with grace in your hearts to the Lord.
Gal 6:1
Brethren, if a man be overtaken in a fault, ye which are spiritual, restore such an one in the spirit of meekness; considering thyself, lest thou also be tempted.
Pro 27:6
Faithful are the wounds of a friend; but the kisses of an enemy are deceitful.
corruption_summary: A house of white canons whose chapter house outlived its church, and the daily business done in such a room.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the chapter of faults turned into a machinery of humiliation, which the later monastic orders were repeatedly disciplined for, and which has an exact Protestant counterpart wherever accountability becomes surveillance. Paul fixes both the manner and the qualification of the corrector: “ye which are spiritual, restore such an one in the spirit of meekness; considering thyself, lest thou also be tempted” (Gal 6:1). The aim named is restoration, and the corrector is warned about himself in the same breath.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that mutual admonition is a daily ordinance for ordinary Christians, not a specialism of cloisters or of officers. “lest any of you be hardened through the deceitfulness of sin” (Heb 3:13) states the danger that silence creates, and the proverb settles the hierarchy of kindnesses: “Faithful are the wounds of a friend; but the kisses of an enemy are deceitful” (Pro 27:6).
roots_summary: Old English beo leah, bee clearing; Greek parakaleo (G3870), to exhort; Greek noutheteo (G3560), to admonish; Greek katartizo (G2675), to restore or mend; Hebrew yakach (H3198), to reprove.
roots_lines: Old English beo + leah — the bee clearing by the Chelmer.
Greek parakaleo (G3870) — to call alongside, to exhort; “But exhort one another daily” (Heb 3:13).
Greek noutheteo (G3560) — to put in mind, to admonish; “teaching and admonishing one another” (Col 3:16).
Greek katartizo (G2675) — to mend, to restore; “restore such an one in the spirit of meekness” (Gal 6:1).
Hebrew ahab (H157) — to love; “Faithful are the wounds of a friend” (Pro 27:6).
usage: “while it is called To day” (Heb 3:13) — the frequency a chapter house assumed.
“considering thyself, lest thou also be tempted” (Gal 6:1) — the corrector's warning.
“but the kisses of an enemy are deceitful” (Pro 27:6) — the alternative to admonition.

pos: n. (a Premonstratensian abbey in Northamptonshire, founded 1155; it depopulated land for sheep pasture)
etymology: Norse personal name Sula with by, a farmstead or village — Sula's village, a Danelaw name.
biblical_def: Sulby was founded in 1155 by William de Wideville as a house of Premonstratensian canons, and it grew by the ordinary means of its century and county: the consolidation of land into sheep walks. The deserted village of Sulby lies beside the abbey site, and the Midlands are full of such grassed-over house platforms, some cleared by monasteries and more by the landlords who succeeded them. Isaiah pronounced the woe on exactly this and did not soften it: “Woe unto them that join house to house, that lay field to field, till there be no place, that they may be placed alone in the midst of the earth!” (Isa 5:8). Micah names the mechanism, which is not theft by night but acquisition by power: “And they covet fields, and take them by violence; and houses, and take them away: so they oppress a man and his house, even a man and his heritage” (Mic 2:2). The word heritage is the hinge. In Israel the land was allotted and inalienable, which is why Naboth could refuse a king, and why the king who took it heard “Hast thou killed, and also taken possession?” (1Ki 21:19).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines engross as to take the whole, to purchase the whole of a commodity for the purpose of selling at a higher price; and depopulate as to dispeople, to deprive of inhabitants.
webster_full: ENGROSS, v.t. To take the whole; to purchase the whole of any commodity, for the purpose of selling at a higher price.
DEPOPULATE, v.t. To dispeople; to deprive of inhabitants, whether by death or by expulsion.
HERITAGE, n. Inheritance; an estate that passes from an ancestor to an heir by descent or course of law.
ENCLOSURE, n. The act of enclosing; the separation of land from common ground into distinct possessions by a fence.
COVET, v.t. To desire inordinately; to desire that which it is unlawful to obtain or possess.
scriptures: Isa 5:8
Woe unto them that join house to house, that lay field to field, till there be no place, that they may be placed alone in the midst of the earth!
Mic 2:2
And they covet fields, and take them by violence; and houses, and take them away: so they oppress a man and his house, even a man and his heritage.

And thou shalt speak unto him, saying, Thus saith the LORD, Hast thou killed, and also taken possession? And thou shalt speak unto him, saying, Thus saith the LORD, In the place where dogs licked the blood of Naboth shall dogs lick thy blood, even thine.
The land shall not be sold for ever: for the land is mine; for ye are strangers and sojourners with me.
corruption_summary: A house of canons that grew by clearing a village for sheep, and the woe Isaiah pronounced on exactly that.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is enclosure as a religious enterprise. The wool trade made the Cistercians and the white canons rich, and the rich house needed more pasture, and the pasture needed fewer tenants. It was all legal. Isaiah's woe is not aimed at illegality but at the end state, “till there be no place, that they may be placed alone in the midst of the earth” (Isa 5:8) — a man alone on a landscape he has emptied.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the one that made Naboth's refusal lawful and Ahab's seizure murder: “The land shall not be sold for ever: for the land is mine; for ye are strangers and sojourners with me” (Lev 25:23). Freehold is not the Bible's highest category. Every tenure is a tenancy, which is as much a limit on a monastery as on a king.
roots_summary: Norse Sula-by, Sula's farm; Hebrew nachalah (H5159), a heritage; Hebrew chamad (H2530), to covet; Hebrew gazal (H1497), to seize by violence; Hebrew ashaq (H6231), to oppress.
roots_lines: Norse Sula + by — Sula's farmstead, a Danelaw name.
Hebrew chamad (H2530) — to desire, to covet; “And they covet fields” (Mic 2:2).
Hebrew gazal (H1497) — to tear away, to seize; “and take them by violence” (Mic 2:2).
Hebrew ashaq (H6231) — to oppress, to defraud; “so they oppress a man and his house” (Mic 2:2).
Hebrew nachalah (H5159) — an inheritance, a heritage; “even a man and his heritage” (Mic 2:2).
usage: “that join house to house, that lay field to field” (Isa 5:8) — the method, named.
“Hast thou killed, and also taken possession?” (1Ki 21:19) — the question put to the acquirer.
“for the land is mine” (Lev 25:23) — the limit on every title.

pos: n. (a Premonstratensian abbey in Northumberland, founded 1165; the village now stands inside its precinct)
etymology: Old French blanche lande, the white land — probably from the white habit of the Premonstratensian canons, Latin Alba Landa.
biblical_def: Blanchland was founded in 1165 by Walter de Bolbec in a loop of the Derwent among the Northumberland moors, a house of the white canons from whose habit it most likely takes its name. After the dissolution the precinct was not demolished but inhabited: the gatehouse, the abbot's lodging and the claustral buildings became a village, and the surviving chancel and tower became its parish church. A local tradition says a Scottish raiding party once missed the house in the moorland mist and was then drawn back by the bells rung in thanksgiving — a story with no evidence and a sound moral. Whatever the tale is worth, the house itself preaches the Psalter's doctrine of covering: “Thou art my hiding place; thou shalt preserve me from trouble; thou shalt compass me about with songs of deliverance” (Psa 32:7), and “in the time of trouble he shall hide me in his pavilion: in the secret of his tabernacle shall he hide me” (Psa 27:5). The hiding is God's act, and in both psalms the hidden man is then set in the open: “he shall set me up upon a rock” (Psa 27:5).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines covert as a shelter, a defense, a thicket or hiding place; and precinct as the limit, bound or exterior line encompassing a place.
webster_full: COVERT, n. A shelter; a defense. A thicket; a hiding place.
PRECINCT, n. The limit, bound or exterior line encompassing a place; sometimes in the plural, bounds, as the precincts of light.
PAVILION, n. A tent; a temporary movable habitation. In Scripture, the covering of God's presence.
DELIVERANCE, n. Release from captivity, slavery, oppression, or any restraint.
MIST, n. Water falling in very numerous, but fine and almost imperceptible drops; watery vapor condensed.
scriptures: Psa 32:7
Thou art my hiding place; thou shalt preserve me from trouble; thou shalt compass me about with songs of deliverance. Selah.
Psa 27:5
For in the time of trouble he shall hide me in his pavilion: in the secret of his tabernacle shall he hide me; he shall set me up upon a rock.
Psa 91:1
He that dwelleth in the secret place of the most High shall abide under the shadow of the Almighty.
Col 3:3
For ye are dead, and your life is hid with Christ in God.
corruption_summary: An abbey whose precinct became a village, and the Psalter's doctrine of being hidden and then set on a rock.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the providential anecdote used as proof — the mist that hid the canons, the bell that betrayed them, the escape told and retold until it becomes evidence of favour. Scripture reports deliverances and also reports the faithful who were not delivered, in the same chapter and without embarrassment. A piety built on rescue stories has nothing to say on the day the mist does not come.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the hiding promised is in God himself and is not primarily from danger: “For ye are dead, and your life is hid with Christ in God” (Col 3:3). That is said to Christians who were being killed. “He that dwelleth in the secret place of the most High shall abide under the shadow of the Almighty” (Psa 91:1) is the same promise and the same scope — a covering that holds whether or not the raiders ride past.
roots_summary: Old French blanche lande, white land; Hebrew sether (H5643), a covering or secret place; Hebrew tsaphan (H6845), to hide or treasure up; Hebrew sukkah (H5521), a booth or pavilion; Greek krupto (G2928), to hide.
roots_lines: Old French blanche lande — the white land, Latin Alba Landa.
Hebrew sether (H5643) — a covering, a hiding place; “Thou art my hiding place” (Psa 32:7).
Hebrew tsaphan (H6845) — to hide, to store up; “in the secret of his tabernacle shall he hide me” (Psa 27:5).
Hebrew sukkah (H5521) — a booth, a pavilion; “he shall hide me in his pavilion” (Psa 27:5).
Greek krupto (G2928) — to hide, to conceal; “your life is hid with Christ in God” (Col 3:3).
usage: “with songs of deliverance” (Psa 32:7) — the bells, if the story is true.
“he shall set me up upon a rock” (Psa 27:5) — hidden, then exposed on purpose.
“For ye are dead” (Col 3:3) — the hiding that does not depend on mist.

pos: n. (a Cistercian abbey in County Wicklow, Ireland, founded 1148 by Dermot MacMurrough, king of Leinster)
etymology: Irish Bealach Conglais, the road or pass of Cuglas, with the abbey's Latin name Vallis Salutis, the valley of salvation.
biblical_def: Baltinglass was founded in 1148 by Dermot MacMurrough, king of Leinster, as a daughter of Mellifont, and its nave arcade with carved capitals still stands. Its founder is the most consequential man in Irish history: driven out of Leinster in 1166, he crossed to Henry II, did homage, and brought back Norman knights to recover his kingdom, and the island was never again free of them. The abbey was called Vallis Salutis, the valley of salvation, by a man who sought his own salvation from a foreign army. Scripture has a case exactly parallel. Ahaz, pressed by Syria and Israel, “sent messengers to Tiglathpileser king of Assyria, saying, I am thy servant and thy son: come up, and save me out of the hand of the king of Syria” (2Ki 16:7). He got what he asked for and lost everything else. Isaiah pronounced the woe on the whole policy: “Woe to the rebellious children, saith the LORD, that take counsel, but not of me” (Isa 30:1), and named the sin as adding “sin to sin” (Isa 30:1).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines alliance as the union of two or more families or nations by treaty, a league, a confederacy; and auxiliary as helping, aiding, assisting, conducive.
webster_full: ALLIANCE, n. The relation or union between families, contracted by marriage. The union between nations, contracted by compact, treaty or league.
AUXILIARY, a. Helping; aiding; assisting; subsidiary; conducive. Auxiliary troops are troops of one nation hired by another.
CONFEDERACY, n. A league, or covenant; a contract between two or more persons, bodies of men or states, combined in support of each other.
VASSAL, n. A feudatory; a tenant; one who holds land of a superior, and who vows fidelity and homage to him.
SALUTE, v.t. To greet; to hail; to address with expressions of kind wishes.
scriptures: So Ahaz sent messengers to Tiglathpileser king of Assyria, saying, I am thy servant and thy son: come up, and save me out of the hand of the king of Syria, and out of the hand of the king of Israel, which rise up against me.
Isa 30:1
Woe to the rebellious children, saith the LORD, that take counsel, but not of me; and that cover with a covering, but not of my spirit, that they may add sin to sin:
Isa 30:2
That walk to go down into Egypt, and have not asked at my mouth; to strengthen themselves in the strength of Pharaoh, and to trust in the shadow of Egypt!
Isa 31:1

Woe to them that go down to Egypt for help; and stay on horses, and trust in chariots, because they are many; and in horsemen, because they are very strong; but they look not unto the Holy One of Israel, neither seek the LORD!
corruption_summary: The valley of salvation, founded by the king who brought the Normans into Ireland to save him.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the foreign alliance entered from fear and paid for with sovereignty. Isaiah describes the men who do it as covering themselves “with a covering, but not of my spirit” (Isa 30:1), which is a precise account of an arrangement that looks like protection and is a transfer of ownership. Dermot got his kingdom back and his successors were tenants.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the object of trust in a genuine emergency, where the temptation is strongest and the alternative looks like doing nothing. “Woe to them that go down to Egypt for help; and stay on horses, and trust in chariots, because they are many” (Isa 31:1) is followed by the charge that they “but they look not unto the Holy One of Israel, neither seek the LORD” (Isa 31:1). The sin is not the diplomacy. It is the not-asking.
roots_summary: Irish Bealach Conglais, the pass of Cuglas; Latin Vallis Salutis, valley of salvation; Hebrew ezrah (H5833), help; Hebrew etsah (H6098), counsel; Hebrew tsel (H6738), a shadow.
roots_lines: Irish Bealach Conglais — the pass of Cuglas, the place name.
Latin Vallis Salutis — the valley of salvation, the abbey's Cistercian name.
Hebrew etsah (H6098) — counsel, advice; “that take counsel, but not of me” (Isa 30:1).
Hebrew tsel (H6738) — a shadow, shelter; “and to trust in the shadow of Egypt” (Isa 30:2).
Hebrew ezrah (H5833) — help, succour; “Woe to them that go down to Egypt for help” (Isa 31:1).
usage: “I am thy servant and thy son” (2Ki 16:7) — the price of the rescue.
“that they may add sin to sin” (Isa 30:1) — the policy, judged.
“neither seek the LORD” (Isa 31:1) — the omission that makes it sin.

pos: n. (a Cistercian abbey in County Kilkenny, Ireland, founded about 1180; famous for the carved figures of its fifteenth-century cloister)
etymology: From Irish Sear Phointe or a Norman-French form of the place on the Little Arrigle, with the Latin name Jeripons.
biblical_def: Jerpoint, founded about 1180 and Cistercian from 1180 as a daughter of Baltinglass, is the best preserved of the Irish Cistercian houses. Its glory is the cloister arcade rebuilt in the fifteenth century, whose double shafts carry carved figures: knights and their ladies, bishops, abbots, a man with toothache, saints with their emblems, and a row of mourners. They are stiff, provincial and unforgettable, and they turn a walking place into a gallery of the dead and the living together. Scripture gives such a gallery a name and a purpose. Hebrews gathers the faithful of every age and sets them around the living church: “seeing we also are compassed about with so great a cloud of witnesses, let us lay aside every weight, and the sin which doth so easily beset us” (Heb 12:1). The witnesses are not spectators enjoying the race; the word is the one for those who have testified. And the direction of the runner's eye is specified immediately: “Looking unto Jesus the author and finisher of our faith” (Heb 12:2).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines cloister as a peristyle or arcade; and witness as testimony, and one who sees or knows a thing and can give evidence of it.
webster_full: CLOISTER, n. A peristyle; a piazza; an arcade. A monastery or nunnery.
WITNESS, n. Testimony; attestation of a fact or event. A person who knows or sees any thing; one personally present.
ARCADE, n. A long or continued arch; a walk arched above.
EFFIGY, n. The image or likeness of a person; resemblance; representation.
BESET, v.t. To surround; to inclose; to hem in; to besiege. To fall upon.
scriptures: Heb 12:1

Wherefore seeing we also are compassed about with so great a cloud of witnesses, let us lay aside every weight, and the sin which doth so easily beset us, and let us run with patience the race that is set before us,
Heb 12:2
Looking unto Jesus the author and finisher of our faith; who for the joy that was set before him endured the cross, despising the shame, and is set down at the right hand of the throne of God.

These all died in faith, not having received the promises, but having seen them afar off, and were persuaded of them, and embraced them, and confessed that they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth.
Rev 7:9

After this I beheld, and, lo, a great multitude, which no man could number, of all nations, and kindreds, and people, and tongues, stood before the throne, and before the Lamb, clothed with white robes, and palms in their hands;
corruption_summary: A cloister whose pillars carry a carved crowd of the dead, and the cloud of witnesses that is not a crowd of spectators.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the conversion of the witnesses into patrons — from men who testified to God's faithfulness into intercessors to be addressed. The carvings at Jerpoint are mostly donors and saints, and the devotional practice that surrounded them turned remembrance into petition. Hebrews gives the witnesses no such office; it uses them as evidence that the race can be run, and sends the runner's eyes elsewhere.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the honest status of the witnesses themselves, who “died in faith, not having received the promises, but having seen them afar off” (Heb 11:13). They are not finished and crowned ahead of us in a different economy; they waited as we wait. The end of the gallery is John's, where no one is carved and “a great multitude, which no man could number, of all nations, and kindreds, and people, and tongues” (Rev 7:9) stands before the throne.
roots_summary: Latin Jeripons, the place name; Greek nephos (G3509), a cloud; Greek martus (G3144), a witness; Greek euperistatos (G2139), easily besetting; Greek teleiotes (G5051), a finisher.
roots_lines: Latin Jeripons — the abbey's name in its own charters.
Greek nephos (G3509) — a cloud, a dense throng; “compassed about with so great a cloud of witnesses” (Heb 12:1).
Greek martus (G3144) — a witness, one who testifies.
Greek euperistatos (G2139) — easily surrounding, besetting; “the sin which doth so easily beset us” (Heb 12:1).
Greek teleiotes (G5051) — a completer, a finisher; “the author and finisher of our faith” (Heb 12:2).
usage: “let us lay aside every weight” (Heb 12:1) — what a gallery of the dead is for.
“Looking unto Jesus” (Heb 12:2) — where the eyes go instead.
“but having seen them afar off” (Heb 11:13) — the status of the carved crowd.

pos: n. (a Cistercian abbey in County Wexford, Ireland, founded 1182; its site was first reported unfit by the monk sent to survey it)
etymology: Irish Dun Bruadair, Bruadar's fort, with the abbey's Latin name Portus Sancti Salvatoris, the harbour of the holy Saviour.
biblical_def: Dunbrody was founded in 1182 on the Barrow estuary in Wexford by Hervey de Montmorency, uncle of Strongbow, as a daughter of St Mary's Dublin and ultimately of Buildwas. The story told of its founding is that the monk first sent over to inspect the grant came back with a bleak report — the land was woodland and marsh, fit for wolves rather than men — and the foundation went ahead regardless. The great cruciform church still stands almost to its full height. The pattern is the oldest in Israel's history. Ten men came back from Canaan and “brought up an evil report of the land which they had searched unto the children of Israel” (Num 13:32). Two came back from the same ground and said “The land, which we passed through to search it, is an exceeding good land” (Num 14:7). The difference between the reports was not information. Caleb and Joshua saw the same giants and added one fact the others left out: “their defence is departed from them, and the LORD is with us: fear them not” (Num 14:9).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines report as an account returned, a statement or relation of facts given in reply to inquiry; and survey as to overlook, to view with a scrutinizing eye, to examine.
webster_full: REPORT, n. An account returned; a statement or relation of facts given in reply to inquiry, or made by a person authorized to examine and make return.
SURVEY, v.t. To overlook; to view with a scrutinizing eye; to examine. To measure and ascertain the boundaries and quantity of a parcel of land.
ESTUARY, n. An arm of the sea; a frith; a narrow passage, or the mouth of a river or lake where the tide meets the current.
DESOLATE, a. Destitute or deprived of inhabitants; desert; uninhabited.
HARBOR, n. A lodging; a place of entertainment and rest. A port or haven for ships.
scriptures: And they brought up an evil report of the land which they had searched unto the children of Israel, saying, The land, through which we have gone to search it, is a land that eateth up the inhabitants thereof; and all the people that we saw in it are men of a great stature.
Num 14:7
And they spake unto all the company of the children of Israel, saying, The land, which we passed through to search it, is an exceeding good land.
Num 14:9
Only rebel not ye against the LORD, neither fear ye the people of the land; for they are bread for us: their defence is departed from them, and the LORD is with us: fear them not.
And Caleb stilled the people before Moses, and said, Let us go up at once, and possess it; for we are well able to overcome it.
corruption_summary: An abbey whose first surveyor called the ground fit for wolves, and the ten spies whose report was accurate and faithless.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the faithless report that is factually true. The ten spies did not invent the giants, and the monk at Dunbrody did not invent the marsh. Scripture calls their account “an evil report” (Num 13:32) anyway, because a survey that leaves God out of the inventory is not neutral reporting; it is a theological claim presented as data. Every committee that kills a work with accurate discouragement is in that company.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is Caleb's method, which was not optimism. He told them “Let us go up at once, and possess it; for we are well able to overcome it” (Num 13:30) with the giants fully in view and the LORD counted in. The faith in question is not about the odds; it is about who else is on the ground.
roots_summary: Irish Dun Bruadair, Bruadar's fort; Latin Portus Sancti Salvatoris, the Saviour's harbour; Hebrew dibbah (H1681), a slander or evil report; Hebrew tur (H8446), to search out; Hebrew yakol (H3201), to be able.
roots_lines: Irish Dun Bruadair — Bruadar's fort on the Barrow.
Latin Portus Sancti Salvatoris — the harbour of the holy Saviour.
Hebrew dibbah (H1681) — whispering, an evil report; “brought up an evil report of the land” (Num 13:32).
Hebrew tur (H8446) — to explore, to search out; “The land, which we passed through to search it” (Num 14:7).
Hebrew yakol (H3201) — to be able, to prevail; “for we are well able to overcome it” (Num 13:30).
usage: “a land that eateth up the inhabitants thereof” (Num 13:32) — accurate, and still an evil report.
“is an exceeding good land” (Num 14:7) — the same ground, counted differently.
“and the LORD is with us: fear them not” (Num 14:9) — the fact the ten omitted.
